taxonomy.note: Current Kew/POWO and Flora of North America accept Rhus copallinum var. lanceolata. The familiar Texas name Rhus lanceolata is a homotypic synonym and should remain prominent in the learner.

evidence: Hays — UT Plant Resources Center Flora of Purola Preserve lists Rhus lanceolata among naturally occurring Anacardiaceae; current Kew treats that name as a homotypic synonym of R. copallinum var. lanceolata.
Travis — UT Plant Resources Center Travis County herbarium index includes Rhus lanceolata; the homotypic synonym maps unambiguously to current R. copallinum var. lanceolata.
Williamson — UT Plant Resources Center Vascular Plants of Williamson County provides a detailed field treatment under Rhus lanceolata.
target_zone_range.guardrail: No county inferred from statewide distribution or nursery/horticultural availability. Synonym-based county evidence is counted only where the synonym maps unambiguously to the current taxon concept.

morphology.look_here_first: Start with the compound leaf: many narrow lance-shaped leaflets sit along a conspicuously winged rachis. Then confirm the deciduous, clonal shrub/small-tree habit and vivid red fall color.
diagnostic_traits: deciduous clonal shrub or small tree, often thicket-forming
odd-pinnate leaves with usually about 13–21 narrow lanceolate leaflets
rachis conspicuously winged between leaflet pairs
leaflets glossy/darker above and paler to hairy below
dioecious; dense terminal branched flower panicles
dark red hairy flattened drupes in dense pyramidal clusters
foliage characteristically turns vivid red/orange in fall

confusers.separator: Evergreen sumac has far fewer (usually 5–9), thicker glossy leaflets and retains foliage through winter; flameleaf has many narrow leaflets, a strongly winged rachis, and is deciduous.
Fragrant sumac has only 3 leaflets and is a low suckering shrub; flameleaf has many leaflets on a long winged rachis and usually develops into a tall shrub/small tree.
